title: 7 · Genotypes
text:
Ranking genotypes
For each year, the predicted and APSIM biomass of the 199 genotypes on a fixed day are compared by the Spearman correlation and by the overlap of the top 10%.

RPython


## Pd, Yd: genotype x year matrices of predicted and APSIM biomass on one
## day. For each year: Spearman correlation of the two rankings and overlap
## of the predicted and true top 10 %.
rank_scores <- function(Pd, Yd, top = 0.1) {
  k <- max(1, round(top * nrow(Yd)))
  score <- function(y) {
    overlap <- intersect(order(-Pd[, y])[1:k], order(-Yd[, y])[1:k])
    data.frame(year = y, rho = cor(Pd[, y], Yd[, y], method = "spearman"),
               top = length(overlap) / k)
  }
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(Yd)), score))
}


# Pd, Yd: genotype x year matrices of predicted and APSIM biomass on one
# day. For each year: Spearman correlation of the two rankings and overlap
# of the predicted and true top 10 %.
def rank_scores(Pd, Yd, top=0.1):
    from scipy.stats import spearmanr
    k = max(1, round(top * Yd.shape[0]))
    rho, overlap = [], []
    for s in range(Yd.shape[1]):
        rho.append(spearmanr(Pd[:, s], Yd[:, s])[0])
        best = set(np.argsort(-Pd[:, s])[:k]) & set(np.argsort(-Yd[:, s])[:k])
        overlap.append(len(best) / k)
    return np.array(rho), np.array(overlap)




RPython

    s <- rank_scores(P[, , i], tr$Y[, , i])
    data.frame(das = i + tr$das0 - 1, rho = mean(s$rho), top10 = mean(s$top))
}
ranking <- do.call(rbind, lapply(days, scores))
ranking[, c("rho", "top10")] <- round(ranking[, c("rho", "top10")], 3)
ranking

title: 7 · Genotypes
5 · Validation
text:
The fitted coefficients \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\) can be used to predict the biomass trajectory of a genotype in a year, given the drivers of that year:
\[\begin{align*}
\dfrac{d\hat y}{dt} &= \boldsymbol{\theta}\bigl(\mathbf{u}(t)\bigr)^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}},
\quad \hat y(t_0) = y_0
\end{align*}\]
This equation can be solved with a standard ODE solver: deSolve::ode (LSODA) in R and scipy.integrate.solve_ivp (LSODA) in Python.

RPython


## Solves dy/dt = (1, theta(y, u)) coef. coef: year x (1 + terms), U: year
## x day x variable. terms(y, u) is the library; by default U is the library.
simulate <- function(coef, U, y0, terms = function(y, u) u, method = "lsoda") {
  S <- dim(U)[1]; D <- dim(U)[2]
  days <- lapply(seq_len(D), function(j) matrix(U[, j, ], S))
  b0 <- coef[, 1]; B <- coef[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  rhs <- function(t, y, parms) {
    pos <- min(max(t + 0.5, 0), D - 1)      # day j is placed at time j - 3/2
    j <- min(floor(pos), D - 2)
    w <- pos - j                            # linear interpolation between days
    u <- (1 - w) * days[[j + 1]] + w * days[[j + 2]]
    list(b0 + .rowSums(terms(y, u) * B, S, ncol(B)))
  }
  deSolve::ode(y0, 0:(D - 1), rhs, NULL, method = method, rtol = 1e-4,
               atol = 1e-4)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
}


# Solves dy/dt = (1, theta(y, u)) coef. coef: year x (1 + terms), U: year
# x day x variable. terms(y, u) is the library; by default U is the library.
def simulate(coef, U, y0, terms=lambda y, u: u, method="LSODA"):
    D = U.shape[1]

    def rhs(t, y):
        pos = min(max(t + 0.5, 0.0), D - 1.0)   # day j is placed at time j - 3/2
        j = min(int(pos), D - 2)
        w = pos - j                             # linear interpolation
        u = (1 - w) * U[:, j] + w * U[:, j + 1]
        return coef[:, 0] + np.einsum("sk,sk->s", terms(y, u), coef[:, 1:])

    return solve_ivp(rhs, (0, D - 1), y0, method=method, t_eval=np.arange(D),
                     rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4).y



If a library depends on the state, terms(y, u) is evaluated along the solution; by default the library depends on the drivers only.

title: 5 · Validation
text:
Leave-one-year-out cross-validation
Each genotype has trajectories in the years \(E\). A year \(e\) is predicted by a model that has not seen it:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\textbf{for each genotype } g, \textbf{ for each year } e \in E: & \\[2pt]
\quad \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(-e)} \leftarrow \texttt{fit}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(-e)},\, \dot{\mathbf{y}}^{(-e)}\bigr) & \text{fit on the other years} \\[2pt]
\quad \bar{y}_0^{(-e)} \leftarrow \tfrac{1}{|E|-1} \textstyle\sum_{e' \ne e} y_0^{(e')} & \text{mean initial biomass} \\[2pt]
\quad \dfrac{d\hat y}{dt} = \boldsymbol{\theta}\bigl(\mathbf{u}^{(e)}(t)\bigr)^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(-e)}, \quad \hat y(t_0) = \bar{y}_0^{(-e)} & \text{predict year } e \text{ from its drivers}
\end{array}
\]
Only the drivers of the left-out year enter the prediction. The error is the root-mean-square error (RMSE, t/ha) over whole trajectories and at maturity.

RPython


## Each year is predicted by a model fitted to the other years of the same
## genotype, starting from the mean initial biomass of those years.
## Returns P[genotype, year, day].
cross_validate <- function(Theta, tr, fit, genotypes = tr$genotypes) {
  P <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr$Y))
  S <- length(tr$years)
  for (g in match(genotypes, tr$genotypes)) {
    d <- make_design(Theta, tr, tr$genotypes[g])
    coef <- t(sapply(seq_len(S), function(v) {
      train <- d$year != v
      fit(d$Theta[train, ], d$dy[train])
    }))
    y0 <- (sum(tr$Y[g, , 1]) - tr$Y[g, , 1]) / (S - 1)
    P[g, , ] <- t(simulate(coef, Theta, y0))
  }
  P
}

## RMSE over whole trajectories, on a fixed day (array index; 99 is day 113
## after sowing) and at maturity. Genotypes that were not predicted are ignored.
evaluate <- function(P, tr, fixed_day = 99) {
  err <- P - tr$Y
  err[, , 1] <- NA                                # the initial value is given
  last <- cbind(as.vector(row(tr$nend)), as.vector(col(tr$nend)),
                as.vector(tr$nend) + 1)
  rmse <- function(e) sqrt(mean(e^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  c(trajectory_rmse = rmse(err), fixed_day_rmse = rmse(err[, , fixed_day]),
    maturity_rmse = rmse(err[last]))
}


# Each year is predicted by a model fitted to the other years of the same
# genotype, starting from the mean initial biomass of those years.
# Returns P[genotype, year, day].
def cross_validate(Theta, tr, fit, genotypes=None):
    P = np.full(tr.Y.shape, np.nan)
    S = len(tr.years)
    for g in (tr.genotypes if genotypes is None else genotypes):
        i = list(tr.genotypes).index(g)
        d = make_design(Theta, tr, g)
        coef = np.array([fit(d.Theta[d.year != s], d.dy[d.year != s])
                         for s in range(S)])
        y0 = (tr.Y[i, :, 0].sum() - tr.Y[i, :, 0]) / (S - 1)
        P[i] = simulate(coef, Theta.array, y0)
    return P


# RMSE over whole trajectories, on a fixed day (days after sowing) and at
# maturity. Genotypes that were not predicted are ignored.
def evaluate(P, tr, fixed_day=113):
    err = P - tr.Y
    err[:, :, 0] = np.nan                        # the initial value is given
    g, s = np.indices(tr.nend.shape)

    def rmse(e):
        return np.sqrt(np.nanmean(e ** 2))

    return {"trajectory_rmse": rmse(err),
            "fixed_day_rmse": rmse(err[:, :, fixed_day - tr.das0]),
            "maturity_rmse": rmse(err[g, s, tr.nend])}

Drivers
The library is built from all eight variables of step 2, Tmin, Tmax, Rain, RAD, VP, DL, TT and RAW, standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. They are here denoted as \(u_1, \dots, u_8\).

RPython


make_drivers <- function(wx, drivers = c("Tmin", "Tmax", "Rain", "RAD", "VP", "DL",
                                          "TT", "RAW")) {
  years <- sort(unique(wx$year))
  das0 <- min(wx$das)
  nd <- max(wx$das) - das0 + 1
  U <- array(NA_real_, c(length(years), nd, length(drivers)),
             dimnames = list(years, NULL, drivers))
  for (j in seq_along(drivers)) {
    i <- cbind(match(wx$year, years), wx$das - das0 + 1, j)
    U[i] <- wx[[drivers[j]]]
  }
  # pad years that end early with their last value
  for (y in seq_along(years)) {
    for (j in seq_along(drivers)) {
      u <- U[y, , j]
      U[y, is.na(u), j] <- tail(u[!is.na(u)], 1)
    }
  }
  center <- apply(U, 3, mean)
  scale <- apply(U, 3, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
  list(U = sweep(sweep(U, 3, center), 3, scale, "/"), years = years,
       das0 = das0, drivers = drivers, center = center, scale = scale)
}


def make_drivers(wx, drivers=DRIVERS):
    years = np.sort(wx["year"].unique())
    das0 = wx["das"].min()
    U = np.full((len(years), wx["das"].max() - das0 + 1, len(drivers)), np.nan)
    y = np.searchsorted(years, wx["year"])
    U[y, (wx["das"] - das0).to_numpy(), :] = wx[drivers].to_numpy()
    for s in range(len(years)):                  # years end on different days
        for j in range(len(drivers)):            # pad with the last value
            u = U[s, :, j]
            u[np.isnan(u)] = u[~np.isnan(u)][-1]
    center = U.mean(axis=(0, 1))
    scale = U.std(axis=(0, 1))
    return Drivers(U=(U - center) / scale, years=years, das0=das0,
                           drivers=list(drivers), center=center, scale=scale)

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Design matrix
For one genotype, the rows of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) are the days of all years and the columns are the library terms. Biomass is recorded at the end of a day, so the weather of day \(i\) drives the change from observation \(i-1\) to \(i\). The vector \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\) holds the growth rate estimates for days \(i\):
\[
\dot y_i = \frac{dy}{dt}(t_{i-1/2}) \approx \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{\Delta t},
\]
and row \(i\) of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) is the library of day \(i\).



The regression problem for genotype g114 as a table: the first three rows of each of the years 1, 2 and 31 (1983, 1984 and 2013). The highlighted row is one equation, \(\dot y_i = \sum_j \Theta_{ij}\xi_j\). The columns of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) are standardised; the coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) are unknown and are estimated in step 4.



RPython


## Rows: days 2, ..., n + 1 of every year. Row i of Theta is the library of day i;
## dy[i] = y_i - y_(i-1) is the growth rate in the middle of day i.
make_design <- function(Theta, tr, genotype) {
  g <- match(genotype, tr$genotypes)
  n <- tr$nend[g, ]
  years <- seq_along(tr$years)
  rows <- lapply(years, function(y) Theta[y, 2:(n[y] + 1), ])
  dy <- lapply(years, function(y) diff(tr$Y[g, y, 1:(n[y] + 1)]))
  rows <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  colnames(rows) <- dimnames(Theta)[[3]]
  list(Theta = rows, dy = unlist(dy), year = rep(years, n))
}


# Rows: days 2, ..., n + 1 of every year. Row i of Theta is the library of day i;
# dy[i] = y_i - y_(i-1) is the growth rate in the middle of day i.
def make_design(Theta, tr, genotype):
    g = list(tr.genotypes).index(genotype)
    n = tr.nend[g]
    years = range(len(tr.years))
    A = Theta.array
    rows = np.vstack([A[s, 1:n[s] + 1, :] for s in years])
    dy = np.concatenate([np.diff(tr.Y[g, s, :n[s] + 1]) for s in years])
    year = np.repeat(np.arange(len(tr.years)), n)
    return Design(Theta=rows, dy=dy, year=year, terms=Theta.terms)

title: 1 · Method
1 · Method
1 · Method
text:
Model
Let \(\mathbf{y}(t)\) denote the state of the crop (for example biomass or leaf area index) and \(\mathbf{u}(t) = (u_1(t), \dots, u_m(t))\) the environmental drivers. The growth of the crop is described by a system of ordinary differential equations:
\[
\dot{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}).
\]
The growth rate \(r\) of one state variable \(y\) (a component of \(\mathbf{y}\), for example biomass) is expressed as a combination of candidate functions \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_K\) (the library),
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = r(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}) \approx \sum_{j=1}^{K} \xi_j\,\theta_j(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u})^\top \boldsymbol{\xi},
\]
where most coefficients \(\xi_j\) are expected to be zero (i.e., not all the candidate functions are necessary to explain the growth rate). The library contains candidate functions (inspired by crop physiology) that may be relevant to explain the growth rate. Furthermore, we can include flexible functions of the drivers, for example splines or polynomials, to capture unknown relationships. The coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) are estimated from the data by regression.



Schematic visualization of the methodology. Environmental drivers \(U\) and the crop state \(Y\) are measured over time. The estimated growth rate of \(Y\) is regressed on a library \(\Theta(Y, U)\) of candidate functions; a sparse coefficient matrix \(\Xi\) selects the terms of the equation. Figure from our preprint (Verburg, Heinlein, van Eeuwijk and Budko, 2026), Physiology-Informed Sparse Identification of Dynamic Crop Models.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Regression
Let \(y_i = y(t_i)\) be the observation at the end of day \(i\), with time step \(\Delta t\) (one day). The weather of day \(i\) acts during that day, so its growth rate belongs to the middle of the day, \(t_{i-1/2} = t_i - \Delta t/2\). It is estimated from the two records enclosing the day,
\[
\dot y_i := \frac{dy}{dt}(t_{i-1/2}) \approx \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{\Delta t}.
\]
The first observation of a trajectory has no earlier observation and gives no growth rate. Routines for this are available in standard packages (numpy.diff in Python, diff in R).



Observed biomass of one genotype in one year (a). The box is enlarged in (b): the slope of the line through the observations at the start and end of day \(i\) estimates \(\dot y_i\), the growth rate in the middle of the day. The growth rates of the whole year are shown in (c); the regression is performed on these.


Collecting all the growth rates in a vector \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\) and the library values in a matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) with entries \(\Theta_{ij} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{u}_i)\) gives
\[
\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
The state \(\mathbf{y}_i\) in the library is the observed state on day \(t_i\). If data are collected in several environments and for several genotypes, the growth rates and library values are stacked. With \(\theta_{i,j}^{(g, e)} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i^{(g, e)}, \mathbf{u}_i^{(g, e)})\) for genotype \(g\) in environment \(e\) on day \(i\):
\[
{\small
\begin{pmatrix}
\dot y_1^{(1, 1)} \\ \vdots \\ \dot y_n^{(1, 1)} \\ \vdots \\ \dot y_n^{(g, e)}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
\theta_{1,1}^{(1, 1)} & \dots & \theta_{1,K}^{(1, 1)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\theta_{n,1}^{(1, 1)} & \dots & \theta_{n,K}^{(1, 1)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\theta_{n,1}^{(g, e)} & \dots & \theta_{n,K}^{(g, e)}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi_1 \\ \vdots \\ \xi_K
\end{pmatrix}
}
\]
The coefficients enter linearly (recall \(\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi}\)), so we just need to solve a linear regression problem to estimate them, for example by least squares:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 .
\]
However, any regression method can be used. We will compare several methods in the workshop.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Making predictions
Given a fitted vector of coefficients \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\), the drivers \(\mathbf{u}(t)\) of a year and an initial state \(\mathbf{y}_0\), the state is predicted by solving the ODE with the estimated coefficients, using an ODE solver of our choice (for example scipy.integrate.solve_ivp in Python or deSolve::ode in R):
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u})^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}, \qquad \mathbf{y}(t_0) = \mathbf{y}_0.
\]
If the library depends on the drivers only, the solution is the integral of the predicted growth rate, \(y(t) = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{u}(s))^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \, ds\), as in the figure.



Year 1998 of one genotype, predicted by a model fitted to the other years. With a library that depends on the drivers only, the predicted growth rate (a) is integrated from the initial value \(y_0\): the shaded area up to day \(t\) is the predicted increase in biomass, \(y(t) - y_0\) (b), which is compared with the APSIM trajectory.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Dealing with multiple genotypes
We can solve the regression problem for each genotype separately, which gives a vector of coefficients \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(g)}\) for each genotype \(g\):
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(g)} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}}^{(g)} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(g)}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 .
\]
The environments and the library are shared, so the columns of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Xi}} = \bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(1)}, \dots, \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(G)}\bigr)\) are directly comparable: each column is the growth equation of one genotype, and the differences between columns describe how genotypes differ in their response to the drivers.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Validation
To test the predictive ability of the model, we can use leave-one-environment-out cross-validation. We calibrate the model on all but one environment, and then predict the left-out environment. This is repeated for each environment, and the predictions are compared with the observed values.



Leave-one-year-out cross-validation. Each row is one fit: the model is fitted to the years in blue and used to predict the left-out year in red.

Constructed variables
Two further variables in the table are constructed from the weather variables: thermal time (TT) and relative available water (RAW).

  TT thermal time\(\sum_{s \le t} \max\left(\tfrac{T_{\min,s} + T_{\max,s}}{2}, 0\right)\)

Thermal time is a measure for the development of the plant, and is computed as the sum of the daily mean temperature, here with base temperature 0\(^\circ\)C, over the days since sowing:
\[
\mathrm{TT}_t = \sum_{s \le t} \max\left(\frac{T_{\min,s} + T_{\max,s}}{2},\, 0\right).
\]
Relative available water is approximated by a simple soil moisture model: rain adds water and a fraction \(k\) of the reference evapotranspiration \(\mathrm{ET}_0\) removes it, up to the capacity \(W_{\max}\) of the soil,
\[
W_t = \min\bigl(\max(W_{t-1} + P_t - k\,\mathrm{ET}_{0,t},\, 0),\, W_{\max}\bigr), \qquad \mathrm{RAW}_t = \frac{W_t}{W_{\max}}.
\]
The maximum available water capacity \(W_{\max} = 217.5\) mm is a property of the soil, and the initial available water \(W_0 = 175\) mm is a property of the season. In this formula. Furthermore, \(\mathrm{ET}_0\) is the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith reference evapotranspiration, computed from the weather variables of the table, and \(k = 0.8\).
So, in total we use eight variables: the six weather variables and the two constructed ones. All of them are candidates for the library.

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
So far, we constructed the library of candidate terms \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) and the growth rates \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\). The next step is to find the coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) that best explain the growth rates as a linear combination of the terms:
\[
\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
We are free to choose any method to fit the coefficients,. The methods differ in how they handle correlated terms, and in whether they produce sparse equations (with some coefficients set exactly to zero).

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
Methods

Least squaresRidgeLassoElastic netBest subsetBackward eliminationSTLSQ


Reference model. OLS does not impose any sparsity.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2
\]
Hyperparameters: none.
R: lm.fit. Python: numpy.linalg.lstsq.

RPython


fit_ols <- function(Theta, dy) {
  Z <- cbind(`1` = 1, Theta)
  drop(solve(crossprod(Z), crossprod(Z, dy)))
}


def fit_ols(Theta, dy):
    return np.linalg.lstsq(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(dy)), Theta]), dy,
                           rcond=None)[0]





Shrinks the coefficients towards zero. This can help to deal with colinearity, but does not produce a sparse equation.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\lambda\): strength of the penalty; shrinks the coefficients.

Closed form, with the penalty scaled as in glmnet.

RPython


## Ridge in closed form, with the penalty scaling of glmnet.
fit_ridge <- function(Theta, dy, lambda = 1e-3) {
  n <- nrow(Theta); mx <- colMeans(Theta)
  var_x <- col_sd(Theta)^2 * (n - 1) / n
  sy <- sd(dy) * sqrt((n - 1) / n)
  b <- solve(crossprod(Theta) / n - tcrossprod(mx) + diag(lambda / sy * var_x),
             crossprod(Theta, dy) / n - mx * mean(dy))
  c(`1` = mean(dy) - sum(mx * b), setNames(drop(b), colnames(Theta)))
}


# Ridge: closed form, same scaling.
def fit_ridge(Theta, dy, lam=1e-3):
    sx = Theta.std(axis=0)
    Z = (Theta - Theta.mean(axis=0)) / sx
    A = Z.T @ Z / len(dy) + lam / dy.std() * np.eye(Theta.shape[1])
    b = np.linalg.solve(A, Z.T @ (dy - dy.mean()) / len(dy)) / sx
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - Theta.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])





The \(\ell_1\) penalty shrinks the coefficients and sets some to zero, producing a sparse equation.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_1
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\lambda\): strength of the penalty.

R: glmnet. Python: scikit-learn ElasticNet, with the penalty scaled as in glmnet.

RPython


## Lasso and elastic net by glmnet.
fit_glmnet <- function(Theta, dy, alpha, lambda) {
  fit <- glmnet::glmnet(Theta, dy, alpha = alpha, lambda = lambda,
                        type.gaussian = "covariance")
  named(as.vector(coef(fit)), Theta)
}

fit_lasso <- function(Theta, dy, lambda = 3e-4) fit_glmnet(Theta, dy, 1, lambda)


# Lasso and elastic net, with the penalty scaling of glmnet.
def fit_glmnet(Theta, dy, alpha, lam):
    sx = Theta.std(axis=0)
    l1, l2 = lam * alpha, lam * (1 - alpha) / dy.std()
    model = ElasticNet(alpha=l1 + l2, l1_ratio=l1 / (l1 + l2), tol=1e-12,
                       max_iter=100000, precompute=True)
    model.fit((Theta - Theta.mean(axis=0)) / sx, dy - dy.mean())
    b = model.coef_ / sx
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - Theta.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])


def fit_lasso(Theta, dy, lam=3e-4):
    return fit_glmnet(Theta, dy, 1, lam)





A mix of ridge and lasso: sparse like the lasso, but more stable for correlated terms.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \Bigl( \tfrac{1 - \alpha}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \alpha \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_1 \Bigr)
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\lambda\): strength of the penalty.
\(\alpha\): mix ratio of the two penalties (here 0.5).


RPython

  fit <- glmnet::glmnet(Theta, dy, alpha = alpha, lambda = lambda,
                        type.gaussian = "covariance")
  named(as.vector(coef(fit)), Theta)
}

fit_enet <- function(Theta, dy, lambda = 6e-4) fit_glmnet(Theta, dy, 0.5, lambda)


# Lasso and elastic net, with the penalty scaling of glmnet.
def fit_glmnet(Theta, dy, alpha, lam):
    sx = Theta.std(axis=0)
    l1, l2 = lam * alpha, lam * (1 - alpha) / dy.std()
    model = ElasticNet(alpha=l1 + l2, l1_ratio=l1 / (l1 + l2), tol=1e-12,
                       max_iter=100000, precompute=True)
    model.fit((Theta - Theta.mean(axis=0)) / sx, dy - dy.mean())
    b = model.coef_ / sx
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - Theta.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])


def fit_enet(Theta, dy, lam=6e-4):
    return fit_glmnet(Theta, dy, 0.5, lam)





The best model with exactly \(k\) terms, found by searching all subsets. This is the most expensive method, as the number of subsets grows combinatorially with the number of terms.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_0 \le k} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2
\]
Algorithm:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\textbf{for each } S \subset \{1, \dots, K\} \textbf{ with } |S| = k: & \\[2pt]
\quad \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_S \leftarrow \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}_S\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 \\[2pt]
\quad \mathrm{RSS}(S) \leftarrow \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}_S\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_S \rVert_2^2 & \\[2pt]
\textbf{return } \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{S^*} \text{ with } S^* = \arg\min_{S} \mathrm{RSS}(S)
\end{array}
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(k\): number of terms that are kept.


RPython


## Best subset or backward elimination with k terms.
fit_subset <- function(Theta, dy, k = 8, method = "exhaustive") {
  b <- coef(leaps::regsubsets(Theta, dy, nvmax = k, method = method), k)
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(Theta) + 1), c("1", colnames(Theta)))
  full[c("1", names(b)[-1])] <- b
  full
}


# Best subset or backward elimination with k terms, from the Gram matrix.
def fit_subset(Theta, dy, k=8, method="exhaustive"):
    Tc, yc = Theta - Theta.mean(axis=0), dy - dy.mean()
    G, c = Tc.T @ Tc, Tc.T @ yc
    if method == "exhaustive":
        subsets = np.array(list(combinations(range(Theta.shape[1]), k)))
        blocks = G[subsets[:, :, None], subsets[:, None, :]]
        b = np.linalg.solve(blocks, c[subsets][..., None])[..., 0]
        keep = subsets[np.argmax((b * c[subsets]).sum(axis=1))]
    else:
        keep = np.arange(Theta.shape[1])
        while len(keep) > k:
            inv = np.linalg.inv(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)])
            increase = (inv @ c[keep]) ** 2 / np.diag(inv)
            keep = np.delete(keep, np.argmin(increase))
    b = np.zeros(Theta.shape[1])
    b[keep] = np.linalg.solve(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)], c[keep])
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - Theta.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])





A greedy alternative to best subset: start with all terms and repeatedly remove the one that increases the residual error least.
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
S \leftarrow \{1, \dots, K\}  \\[2pt]
\textbf{while } |S| > k: & \\[2pt]
\quad \Delta_j \leftarrow \mathrm{RSS}(S \setminus \{j\}) - \mathrm{RSS}(S) \quad \text{for each } j \in S \\[2pt]
\quad S \leftarrow S \setminus \{j^*\}, \quad j^* = \arg\min_{j \in S} \Delta_j \\[2pt]
\textbf{return } \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_S
\end{array}
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(k\): number of terms that are kept.


RPython


## Best subset or backward elimination with k terms.
fit_subset <- function(Theta, dy, k = 8, method = "exhaustive") {
  b <- coef(leaps::regsubsets(Theta, dy, nvmax = k, method = method), k)
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(Theta) + 1), c("1", colnames(Theta)))
  full[c("1", names(b)[-1])] <- b
  full
}


# Best subset or backward elimination with k terms, from the Gram matrix.
def fit_subset(Theta, dy, k=8, method="exhaustive"):
    Tc, yc = Theta - Theta.mean(axis=0), dy - dy.mean()
    G, c = Tc.T @ Tc, Tc.T @ yc
    if method == "exhaustive":
        subsets = np.array(list(combinations(range(Theta.shape[1]), k)))
        blocks = G[subsets[:, :, None], subsets[:, None, :]]
        b = np.linalg.solve(blocks, c[subsets][..., None])[..., 0]
        keep = subsets[np.argmax((b * c[subsets]).sum(axis=1))]
    else:
        keep = np.arange(Theta.shape[1])
        while len(keep) > k:
            inv = np.linalg.inv(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)])
            increase = (inv @ c[keep]) ** 2 / np.diag(inv)
            keep = np.delete(keep, np.argmin(increase))
    b = np.zeros(Theta.shape[1])
    b[keep] = np.linalg.solve(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)], c[keep])
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - Theta.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])





Sequential thresholded least squares, the algorithm of the original SINDy method.
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
S \leftarrow \{1, \dots, K\} \\[2pt]
\textbf{repeat:} & \\[2pt]
\quad \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_S \leftarrow \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}_S\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2  \\[2pt]
\quad S' \leftarrow \bigl\{ j \in S : |\hat{\xi}_j|\, s_j \ge \tau \bigr\}, \quad s_j = \mathrm{sd}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_j) / \mathrm{sd}\bigl(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\bigr)  \\[2pt]
\quad \textbf{if } S' = S \text{ or } S' = \emptyset \textbf{ then stop, else } S \leftarrow S' & \\[2pt]
\textbf{return } \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_S
\end{array}
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\tau\): threshold on the scaled coefficient \(|\hat{\xi}_j|\,s_j\).


RPython


## Sequential thresholded least squares: refit, drop terms below the threshold.
fit_stlsq <- function(Theta, dy, threshold = 0.05) {
  Z <- cbind(`1` = 1, Theta)
  G <- crossprod(Z)
  rhs <- drop(crossprod(Z, dy))
  size <- col_sd(Theta) / sd(dy)
  active <- colnames(Theta)
  repeat {
    i <- c("1", active)
    b <- drop(solve(G[i, i], rhs[i]))
    keep <- abs(b[-1]) * size[active] >= threshold
    if (all(keep) || !any(keep)) break
    active <- active[keep]
  }
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(Theta) + 1), c("1", colnames(Theta)))
  full[names(b)] <- b
  full
}


# Sequential thresholded least squares: refit, drop terms below the threshold.
def fit_stlsq(Theta, dy, threshold=0.05):
    size = Theta.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / dy.std(ddof=1)
    active = np.arange(Theta.shape[1])
    while True:
        b = fit_ols(Theta[:, active], dy)
        keep = np.abs(b[1:]) * size[active] >= threshold
        if keep.all() or not keep.any():
            break
        active = active[keep]
    full = np.zeros(Theta.shape[1] + 1)
    full[0], full[1 + active] = b[0], b[1:]
    return full

Accumulated local effects (ALE) vary the driver only within narrow intervals around values that occur, using the observed values of the other drivers, and accumulate the resulting changes in the growth rate. For the fitted growth rate \(f(\mathbf{u}) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{u})^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\) and driver \(j\),
\[
\mathrm{ALE}_j(z) = \int_{z_0}^{z} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial f(\mathbf{u})}{\partial u_j} \,\middle|\, u_j = v\right] dv - c,
\]
where \(z_0\) is the smallest observed value and the constant \(c\) centres the curve at mean zero over the data.

section: From data to a regression problem
text:
From data to a regression problem
Let \(y_i = y(t_i)\) be the observation at the end of day \(i\), with time step \(\Delta t\) (one day). We can estimate the growth rate \(\dot y_i\) of the state \(y\) in the middle of day \(i\) by the slope of the line through the observations at the start and end of day \(i\):
\[
\dot y_i := \frac{dy}{dt}(t_{i-1/2}) \approx \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{\Delta t}.
\]
Routines for this are available in standard packages (numpy.diff in Python, diff in R). For noisy data, more advanced methods can be used to estimate the derivative, for example smoothing splines.



Observed biomass of one genotype in one year (a). The box is enlarged in (b): the slope of the line through the observations at the start and end of day \(i\) estimates \(\dot y_i\), the growth rate in the middle of the day. The growth rates of the whole year are shown in (c); the regression is performed on these.


Collecting all the growth rates in a vector \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\) and the library values in a matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) with entries \(\Theta_{ij} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{u}_i)\) gives
\[
\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
The state \(\mathbf{y}_i\) in the library is the observed state on day \(t_i\). If data are collected in several environments and for several genotypes, the growth rates and library values are stacked. With \(\theta_{i,j}^{(g, e)} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i^{(g, e)}, \mathbf{u}_i^{(g, e)})\) for genotype \(g\) in environment \(e\) on day \(i\):
\[
{\small
\begin{pmatrix}
\dot y_1^{(1, 1)} \\ \vdots \\ \dot y_n^{(1, 1)} \\ \vdots \\ \dot y_n^{(g, e)}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
\theta_{1,1}^{(1, 1)} & \dots & \theta_{1,K}^{(1, 1)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\theta_{n,1}^{(1, 1)} & \dots & \theta_{n,K}^{(1, 1)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\theta_{n,1}^{(g, e)} & \dots & \theta_{n,K}^{(g, e)}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi_1 \\ \vdots \\ \xi_K
\end{pmatrix}
}
\]
Note that this is a linear regression problem (recall \(\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi}\)), that can be solved by, e.g., ordinary least squares (OLS) regression:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \boldsymbol{\Theta}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 .
\]
However, any regression method can be used. We will compare several methods in the workshop.
